claims.text: CaH2 activates or decomposes at approximately 800–900°C, overlapping the TaH0.5 decomposition window.
CaH2 decomposition releases hydrogen and produces reactive calcium that is subsequently oxidized to CaO.
The proposed CaH2-assisted regime will completely dehydrogenate the metallic/hydride precursor blend.
The CaH2 getter will reduce oxygen partial pressure below 10^-15 atm.
Lowering oxygen activity below the proposed threshold will prevent alpha-phase nucleation in HfNbTaTiZr.
A transient CaO layer forms on particle surfaces during the treatment.
Local suppression of gas-phase oxygen activity kinetically inhibits nucleation of Ti/Zr-rich alpha-HCP phases.
Oxidation of calcium to CaO scavenges oxygen from the processing environment or alloy.
Rapid quenching suppresses the diffusion-controlled transformation from beta-BCC to alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC.
Rapid quenching from 1250°C will retain metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed treatment will produce greater than 98% theoretical density.
The quenched alloy will have a grain size of 10–20 micrometers.
No detectable alpha-HCP phase or alpha-Ti precipitates will remain after quenching.
The precursor blend initially contains approximately 500–1000 ppm oxygen.
Standard sintering without a reactive getter or with Ti powder leaves more than 200 ppm residual oxygen.
Residual oxygen above 200 ppm leads to a dual alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC microstructure after slow cooling.
Insufficient oxygen removal produces brittle alpha-Ti precipitates even after quenching.
Getter effectiveness depends on temporal overlap between CaH2 activation and the critical hydride-decomposition/alloying window.
Rapid passivation by the forming oxide layer could limit oxygen scavenging and permit trace alpha-phase formation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says CaH2 decomposes to CaO while releasing hydrogen, whereas the mechanism gives a two-step pathway in which CaH2 first decomposes to Ca and H2 and calcium is then separately oxidized to CaO.

The production regime uses a 2°C/min ramp to 900°C with a 2-hour hold and then a 10°C/min ramp to 1250°C with a 30-minute hold, but the proposed verification experiment uses a continuous 5°C/min ramp to 1300°C. Thus, it does not directly reproduce the claimed kinetic regime.
The term 'alpha phase' is used inconsistently for alpha-HCP/alpha-Ti and for an asserted alpha-BCC phase, making the phase transformation and falsification target ambiguous.
